# DataAnnotations — Validate

::: {.callout-note appearance="default" collapse="false"}
**Q:** Can `DataAnnotations` actually throw error (e.g. in IDE, compile time, run time)?
:::

The short answer is: **DataAnnotations do NOT throw errors automatically** - they're just metadata. Let me explain when they actually work:


## How DataAnnotations Actually Work


```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         DataAnnotations Validation Flow                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                           │
│  Compile Time:   ✗ NO validation                        │
│  IDE:            ✗ NO warnings (by default)             │
│  Object Creation: ✗ NO automatic validation             │
│                                                           │
│  Runtime:        ✓ Only when explicitly validated       │
│                  ✓ Or when framework validates          │
│                                                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```


## Example: DataAnnotations DON'T Throw Automatically


```csharp
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

public record Patient
{
    [Required]
    [StringLength(10, MinimumLength = 3)]
    public string Name { get; init; }
    
    [Range(0, 150)]
    public int Age { get; init; }
}

// This compiles fine - NO errors!
var patient1 = new Patient { Name = "", Age = -5 };  // Invalid but NO exception

// This also works - NO errors!
var patient2 = new Patient { Name = "ThisNameIsWayTooLongAndExceedsTenCharacters", Age = 200 };

// Nothing happens - the object is created with invalid data
Console.WriteLine($"Patient created: {patient1.Name}, Age: {patient1.Age}");
// Output: Patient created: , Age: -5
```

**No compile error, no IDE warning, no runtime exception!** The attributes are just sitting there doing nothing.


## When DO They Throw/Validate?


### Option 1: Manual Validation (YOU must call it)


```csharp
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

var patient = new Patient { Name = "", Age = -5 };

// Manual validation
var context = new ValidationContext(patient);
var results = new List<ValidationResult>();

bool isValid = Validator.TryValidateObject(
    patient, 
    context, 
    results, 
    validateAllProperties: true  // Important! Validates all properties
);

if (!isValid)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Validation errors:");
    foreach (var error in results)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"  - {error.ErrorMessage}");
    }
}

// Output:
// Validation errors:
//   - The Name field is required.
//   - The field Age must be between 0 and 150.
```


### Option 2: ASP.NET Core Automatically Validates


When you use DataAnnotations in ASP.NET Core API controllers, the framework validates automatically:

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

// API Controller
[ApiController]
[Route("api/[controller]")]
public class PatientsController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpPost]
    public IActionResult CreatePatient([FromBody] Patient patient)
    {
        // ASP.NET Core AUTOMATICALLY validates patient here
        // If invalid, returns 400 Bad Request with error details
        // You don't reach this code if validation fails!
        
        return Ok(patient);
    }
}

// Request with invalid data:
// POST /api/patients
// { "name": "", "age": -5 }

// Response (automatic 400 error):
// {
//   "type": "https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-6.5.1",
//   "title": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
//   "status": 400,
//   "errors": {
//     "Name": ["The Name field is required."],
//     "Age": ["The field Age must be between 0 and 150."]
//   }
// }
```


### Option 3: Entity Framework Core Validates


EF Core validates DataAnnotations when you try to save to database:

```csharp
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

public class HospitalDbContext : DbContext
{
    public DbSet<Patient> Patients { get; set; }
}

// This will throw exception when SaveChanges is called
var patient = new Patient { Name = "", Age = -5 };

var db = new HospitalDbContext();
db.Patients.Add(patient);

// ❌ THROWS ValidationException here!
await db.SaveChangesAsync();  
// Exception: One or more validation errors occurred
```


## Complete Example: All Scenarios


```csharp
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

public record DicomStudy
{
    [Required(ErrorMessage = "Study Instance UID is required")]
    [RegularExpression(@"^[\d.]+$", ErrorMessage = "Invalid UID format")]
    public string StudyInstanceUID { get; init; }
    
    [Required]
    [StringLength(16, ErrorMessage = "Accession number too long")]
    public string AccessionNumber { get; init; }
    
    [Range(1, 1000, ErrorMessage = "Image count must be 1-1000")]
    public int ImageCount { get; init; }
}

// ─────────────────────────────────────────────
// Scenario 1: Just creating object - NO validation
// ─────────────────────────────────────────────
var study1 = new DicomStudy
{
    StudyInstanceUID = "invalid!@#",  // Wrong format
    AccessionNumber = "ThisIsWayTooLongForAccessionNumber",  // Too long
    ImageCount = 5000  // Out of range
};
Console.WriteLine("Study1 created - no errors!"); // This runs fine!


// ─────────────────────────────────────────────
// Scenario 2: Manual validation - DOES validate
// ─────────────────────────────────────────────
var study2 = new DicomStudy
{
    StudyInstanceUID = "1.2.840.113619.2.55",
    AccessionNumber = "ACC12345",
    ImageCount = 100
};

var context = new ValidationContext(study2);
var results = new List<ValidationResult>();

if (!Validator.TryValidateObject(study2, context, results, true))
{
    Console.WriteLine("Validation failed!");
    results.ForEach(r => Console.WriteLine($"  - {r.ErrorMessage}"));
}
else
{
    Console.WriteLine("Study2 is valid!");
}


// ─────────────────────────────────────────────
// Scenario 3: Throw exception on validation failure
// ─────────────────────────────────────────────
var study3 = new DicomStudy
{
    StudyInstanceUID = "",  // Invalid
    AccessionNumber = "ACC123",
    ImageCount = 50
};

try
{
    // ValidateObject throws exception if invalid
    Validator.ValidateObject(study3, new ValidationContext(study3), true);
    Console.WriteLine("Study3 is valid");
}
catch (ValidationException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"❌ Validation exception: {ex.Message}");
    // Output: ❌ Validation exception: Study Instance UID is required
}
```


## Comparison Table


```
┌────────────────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────┐
│ Context                │ Auto Validate│ Manual Code Needed   │
├────────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Creating object        │ ✗ No         │ N/A - Never validates│
│ (new Patient {...})    │              │                      │
├────────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Manual validation      │ ✗ No         │ ✓ Call Validator     │
│                        │              │   TryValidateObject  │
├────────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ ASP.NET Core           │ ✓ Yes        │ ✗ Automatic (with    │
│ [ApiController]        │              │   [ApiController])   │
├────────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ ASP.NET MVC            │ ✓ Yes        │ ✗ Check ModelState   │
│                        │              │   in controller      │
├────────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Entity Framework Core  │ ✓ Yes        │ ✗ Validates on       │
│ SaveChanges()          │              │   SaveChanges()      │
├────────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Blazor forms           │ ✓ Yes        │ ✗ With DataAnnotations│
│                        │              │   Validator component│
└────────────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────┘
```


## Helper Class for Manual Validation


Here's a utility class you can use to easily validate any object with DataAnnotations:

```csharp
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

public static class DataAnnotationValidator
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Validates an object and returns whether it's valid
    /// </summary>
    public static (bool IsValid, List<string> Errors) Validate<T>(T obj)
    {
        var context = new ValidationContext(obj);
        var results = new List<ValidationResult>();
        
        bool isValid = Validator.TryValidateObject(obj, context, results, validateAllProperties: true);
        
        var errors = results.Select(r => r.ErrorMessage ?? "Unknown error").ToList();
        return (isValid, errors);
    }
    
    /// <summary>
    /// Validates and throws exception if invalid
    /// </summary>
    public static void ValidateAndThrow<T>(T obj)
    {
        var context = new ValidationContext(obj);
        Validator.ValidateObject(obj, context, validateAllProperties: true);
    }
    
    /// <summary>
    /// Validates and returns detailed results
    /// </summary>
    public static List<ValidationResult> ValidateDetailed<T>(T obj)
    {
        var context = new ValidationContext(obj);
        var results = new List<ValidationResult>();
        Validator.TryValidateObject(obj, context, results, validateAllProperties: true);
        return results;
    }
}

// Usage examples:
var study = new DicomStudy { /* ... */ };

// Option 1: Check if valid
var (isValid, errors) = DataAnnotationValidator.Validate(study);
if (!isValid)
{
    errors.ForEach(Console.WriteLine);
}

// Option 2: Throw exception if invalid
try
{
    DataAnnotationValidator.ValidateAndThrow(study);
}
catch (ValidationException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Invalid: {ex.Message}");
}

// Option 3: Get detailed results
var validationResults = DataAnnotationValidator.ValidateDetailed(study);
foreach (var result in validationResults)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Property: {string.Join(", ", result.MemberNames)}");
    Console.WriteLine($"Error: {result.ErrorMessage}");
}
```


## Key Takeaways


1. **DataAnnotations are passive metadata** - they don't do anything by themselves
2. **No compile-time or IDE errors** (unless you use special analyzers)
3. **You must explicitly validate** OR **use a framework that validates for you**
4. **Best for ASP.NET Core APIs** where validation is automatic
5. **For domain models**, consider constructor validation or factory patterns instead
